# Three Miles an Hour

## I. The Door

There is a particular pleasure, available to almost everyone and taken by almost no one, in closing a door behind you without knowing where you're going. Not to the store. Not to the car. Not to the train. Just out. The errand-less walk is one of the last unproductive acts left to us, and it feels faintly illicit for exactly that reason, like playing hooky from your own life.

Everything else in the day has a destination. We wake and are immediately aimed at something — the inbox, the appointment, the task with its little checkbox waiting to be ticked. To leave the house with no target is to break formation. It is a small desertion, and the body knows it. There's a looseness in the shoulders within the first hundred yards, a sense of having gotten away with something.

Here is a number worth thinking about: three miles an hour. That is the native speed of the human animal, the pace our species has been walking for a few million years, give or take a stroll. Everything we have built since — the horse, the sail, the wheel, the piston, the turbine, the rocket — has been an argument with that number, and the argument has been won so completely that we now treat three miles an hour as a form of failure. Stuck in traffic. Delayed. Falling behind.

But the mind, stubborn old organ that it is, never received the upgrade. It still runs best at the original clock speed. And it will wait — patiently, for decades, through every flight and freeway — for you to slow down enough to hear it.

## II. It Is Solved by Walking

The story goes that when Zeno of Elea was arguing that motion was impossible — that an arrow in flight is, at every instant, at rest, and so never moves — the philosopher Diogenes simply stood up and walked away. No counterargument. No treatise. He refuted the paradox with his feet. Later centuries pinned a Latin phrase to the gesture: *solvitur ambulando*. It is solved by walking.

I think about that phrase constantly, because it names something we all know and keep forgetting: there is a category of problems that cannot be argued with, only moved through. Grief is one. Fury is another. The stalled sentence, the decision that won't decide, the 3 a.m. dread that has no object — these do not yield to sitting still and thinking harder. They yield, if they yield at all, to rhythm. Left, right. Left, right. The oldest technology we have for unsticking a mind is the one built into the bottom of it.

Western philosophy understood this at its founding and then, somehow, misplaced the knowledge. Aristotle taught while walking — so the tradition holds — pacing the covered colonnades of the Lyceum in Athens with his students trailing behind him, which is why his school came to be called *Peripatetic*, from *peripatein*, to walk around. Sit with that for a moment. The founding image of Western systematic thought is not a man in an armchair. It is a man in motion, ideas arriving footstep by footstep, the whole enterprise conducted at three miles an hour.

Two millennia later we moved philosophy indoors, sat it at desks, gave it fluorescent lighting and ergonomic chairs, and we wonder why so much of it reads like it was written by people whose bodies had been informed they were no longer needed.

## III. The Engine of Thought

The science, when it finally caught up, confirmed what the walkers always claimed. In 2014, researchers at Stanford — Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz — ran experiments comparing the creative output of people sitting versus people walking. The walkers produced dramatically more novel ideas on standard tests of divergent thinking, roughly sixty percent more on some measures. And here is the detail I love: it worked on a treadmill facing a blank wall. The boost wasn't from scenery, from birdsong, from the romance of the outdoors. It was from the motion itself. The walking was doing something all by itself.

What, exactly? Nobody knows for certain, but the guesses are beautiful. One is that walking occupies the animal just enough — the body gets its little job, its leash of rhythm — and stops interrupting the mind with its restlessness. Walking is precisely the right amount of busy. Too little, and the body fidgets and frets; too much, and all resources go to the effort. At three miles an hour there is a surplus of attention that has nowhere to go but sideways, into association, into the loose connective drift that psychologists call the default mode network and the rest of us call thinking about nothing in particular, which is where, it turns out, nearly everything in particular comes from.

Another guess involves the steady lateral rhythm of walking, the way it resembles certain therapeutic techniques for processing difficult emotion. Another still involves *optic flow* — the world streaming gently past the eyes — which seems to loosen the mind's grip on whatever it's white-knuckling. Whatever the mechanism, the effect is ancient and reliable: the stalled mind, set walking, comes unstuck. The body walks the mind home like a friend who knows when not to talk.

## IV. The Great Walkers

Once you start looking for them, the walkers are everywhere in the history of thought, and they knew exactly what they were doing.

Charles Darwin, after moving to Down House in Kent, had a quarter-mile gravel loop laid out on the property — the Sandwalk, the family called it, or the "thinking path." At the head of the path he kept a pile of flints. Each lap, he kicked one flint onto the path. That way he could allocate his problems without interrupting them: a three-flint problem, a four-flint problem, a five-flint problem — the hardest ones. Think of it. The theory of evolution by natural selection, assembled one kicked stone at a time, the mind keeping its accounts with its feet.

Charles Dickens wrote all day and then walked all night, twenty or thirty miles through London at a ferocious clip, returning at dawn. He told his friend and biographer John Forster that if he could not walk far and fast, he believed he would "explode and perish." Read his novels with this in mind and you see it: they are London rendered at walking speed, an omnibus of doorways, gutters, shopfronts, faces — the city as it appears to someone on foot, in absurd abundance. Virginia Woolf, a generation later, needed an excuse, because respectable women of her time were not supposed to simply roam. So she invented errands. Her essay "Street Haunting" begins with the pretext of going out to buy a pencil — a pencil! — and then unfolds into one of the great celebrations of walking as an escape from the furnished room of the self into the anonymity of the street, where, as she writes, one is no longer quite oneself but part of the enormous army of the anonymous.

William Wordsworth may be the greatest walker in the history of literature. His friend Thomas De Quincey estimated that Wordsworth's legs carried him somewhere between 175,000 and 180,000 miles over his lifetime — seven times around the equator, on foot, mostly up and down the Lake District. He composed aloud while walking, muttering and booming along the paths, and locals grew accustomed to the sound. It cannot be coincidence that his verse marches. Iambic meter is a walking rhythm — da-DUM, da-DUM, left, right. Poetry has *feet*; we say it all the time without hearing it. Wordsworth heard it.

The list runs on. Kierkegaard walked Copenhagen daily and wrote to his niece: "Above all, do not lose your desire to walk. Every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness. I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it." Nietzsche, tramping the Alps with a notebook, went further and got harsher: only thoughts won by walking, he declared, have value. Thoreau insisted on four hours a day minimum, sauntering through the woods "absolutely free from all worldly engagements," and he loved that the word *saunter* might descend either from *Sainte-Terre* — the Holy Land, destination of pilgrims — or from *sans terre*, without land, homeless, at home everywhere. He declined to choose between the etymologies, because a walk, he understood, is both at once: a pilgrimage and a vagrancy, sacred and unhoused in the same stride.

## V. The Connoisseur of Streets

The nineteenth century gave the practice a name and a costume: the *flâneur*, the deliberate wanderer of the city, the connoisseur of streets. Baudelaire sketched the type — the man whose passion and profession, he wrote, is "to become one flesh with the crowd." Not to get anywhere. To *be* somewhere, intensely, on purpose, in public, at a stroll. Walter Benjamin, later, made the flâneur the central figure of his enormous unfinished study of the Paris arcades, those glass-roofed shopping passages that were, he thought, the dream-houses of the industrial age.

Benjamin also preserved the era's most charming legend: that around 1840 it briefly became fashionable among flâneurs to take turtles for walks through the arcades, letting the creatures set the pace. Whether or not anyone actually did this, the story survives because it carries a truth. Flânerie was a discipline of slowness — a refusal of the factory whistle's tempo, of the new religion of efficiency. The turtle was the ideal walking companion for an age that had begun to worship speed, because the turtle enforces the one thing the flâneur exists to protect: the pace at which the world is actually visible.

And that is the flâneur's real creed, still available to any of us: to walk slowly through a world arranged for hurry is a small act of resistance. The city at three miles an hour is a book. The same city at forty is a channel being surfed.

## VI. The Long Walkers

Then there are the walks measured not in hours but in weeks, where walking stops being a pastime and becomes a form of life.

In 1689, the Japanese poet Bashō set out on foot into the deep north of his country — a journey of some fifteen hundred miles over five months, much of it through country considered remote and dangerous. Out of it came *The Narrow Road to the Deep North*, a travel journal in prose and haiku, and one of the quietest, strangest books ever written. Bashō walked to lose himself and find poems, or perhaps the other way around; by the end it is hard to tell the walking from the writing, and that seems to have been the point.

The Camino de Santiago has drawn pilgrims across Spain for over a thousand years, and its modern pilgrims — religious, lapsed, skeptical, brokenhearted — report something consistent: that somewhere around the second week, when the blisters have healed and the pack has lightened and the days have simplified into walk, eat, sleep, the walk stops being something you are doing and becomes something you are. The chatter of the self runs out of material. What remains is simpler and, by most accounts, kinder.

Bruce Chatwin, in *The Songlines*, reported on the songlines of Aboriginal Australia — paths across the continent encoded in song, where the land itself is mapped in melody and the song can only be sung at walking pace, because the verses correspond to features of the ground passing underfoot. Chatwin romanticized, and his book is part invention, but the underlying idea stops me cold: knowledge stored at three miles an hour. A library you can only read with your legs. And it was Chatwin who floated the grand thesis that humans are, at root, the walking animal — that we are built nomadic, that restlessness is not a flaw in our design but the design itself.

John Muir said it best, because he lived it most: "I only went out for a walk, and finally concluded to stay out till sundown, for going out, I found, was really going in."

## VII. Who Gets to Wander

Any honest praise of walking has to pause here and ask an uncomfortable question: who gets to?

The flâneur strolled the arcades in a good coat, with money in his pocket and a home to return to. The same gait in different circumstances has always earned a different name. Wander with resources and you are a flâneur, a pilgrim, a nature writer. Wander without them and you are a vagrant, a loiterer, a suspicious person. Loitering and vagrancy laws have policed the poor's only mode of motion for centuries. A woman walking alone at night performs a constant calculus — of streetlights, of footsteps behind her, of keys held between knuckles — that most men never once consider. A Black man walking through certain American neighborhoods has been stopped, in living memory and in the present tense, for the crime of ambulation in the wrong zip code. The walker's freedom, it turns out, is distributed exactly as unevenly as every other freedom.

And perhaps that is why walking, reclaimed deliberately and collectively, has so often been the grammar of protest. In 1930, Gandhi walked two hundred forty miles to the sea over twenty-four days to make salt, and an empire's logic began to crack with every footstep. The Selma marchers walked fifty-four miles and changed a country. There is something uniquely legible about a crowd moving on foot, slowly, toward power: unarmored, unhurried, impossible to mistake for anything but conviction. The march remains the clearest sentence a public can write.

At three miles an hour, which is the speed at which a human being can bear things.

You return with nothing to show — no purchase, no trophy, no measurable output, nothing for the ledger — except that the furniture inside your head has been rearranged an inch to the left, a window has been cracked open, a knot you had stopped trying to untie is lying loose on the floor.

Going out, Muir said, was really going in.

Diogenes: when Zeno argued motion was impossible, Diogenes stood up and walked away. "Solvitur ambulando" — it is solved by walking. The whole history of philosophy in one gesture. Some problems aren't argued but walked out of.

The peripatetic school — Aristotle lectured while pacing the covered walkways (peripatoi) of the Lyceum. So the founding image of Western thought is not a man in an armchair but a man in motion, students trailing behind, ideas arriving footstep by footstep. Maybe that's why his works read like lecture notes — because they were, written for legs, not desks.

Science: Oppezzo & Schwartz at Stanford, 2014 — walking and divergent thinking, 60% boost, treadmill worked too, and the boost lingered after sitting back down. The mechanism guesses: increased blood flow barely registers as exercise so the mind is free; the steady bilateral rhythm is a metronome for thought; the optic flow of the world sliding past loosens associative thinking. Darwin's Sandwalk: at Down House he laid a gravel quarter-mile loop, the "thinking path," and kept a pile of flints at the start, kicking one onto the path per lap so he could count three-, four-, five-lap problems without breaking his chain of thought. Dickens: walked 20-30 miles through London at night after writing all day; said if he couldn't walk fast and far he would "explode and perish." His novels are London-at-walking-speed, omnibus of street detail. Woolf's "Street Haunting" — the pretext of buying a pencil to justify an evening walk; walking as the escape from the self's room into the great anonymity of the street.

Wordsworth: De Quincey estimated his legs carried him 175,000-180,000 miles. He composed aloud while walking, muttering; the meter of his verse is the meter of the stride. Iambic pentameter is roughly walking rhythm — da-DUM da-DUM, left-right. Poetry has feet. This is literal, not metaphor.

Kierkegaard: walked Copenhagen daily, "I have walked myself into my best thoughts." Nietzsche: "Only ideas won by walking have value" — though he wrote that after walking Alpine paths for hours with a notebook. Thoreau: four hours a day minimum, "sauntering," possibly from "Sainte-Terre" (holy land pilgrim) or "sans terre" (without land) — he liked both etymologies, which tells you walking is both pilgrimage and homelessness, sacred and unhoused at once.

The Aboriginal songlines — Chatwin's telling — country that must be sung at walking pace; the songs are maps encoded in melody; you can't sing them faster than you can walk them. The wanderer with resources is a flâneur; without, a vagrant. Same gait, different verdicts. Gandhi turned walking into revolution — the Salt March, 240 miles, 24 days, each step a political syllable. The march as grammar of protest: Selma, every march since. When people gather to walk slowly and deliberately toward power, it is still the most legible sentence a crowd can write.

Streets used to be commons — markets, playgrounds, parliament — and within a generation they were lanes of traffic with humans permitted at edges and intervals. Suburbs built without sidewalks: neighborhoods where walking is technically possible but semantically absurd. The treadmill invented 1818 by William Cubitt as prison punishment — the "everlasting staircase" — and now we pay monthly fees for gyms to use its descendants, because the world outside has been arranged to make walking unnecessary, which is to say impossible, which is to say sad. Mall walkers: seniors circling food courts at 7 a.m. — the flâneur's last arcade. There's something heartbreaking and defiant about it.

Phones: the walk as the last unscreened hour, now also colonized. The person on the bench staring down. Walking with headphones vs. walking with ears open — I won't moralize too hard, but there's a difference between walking through a place and carrying your elsewhere with you. # Three Miles an Hour

### I. The door

There is a particular pleasure in closing a door behind you without knowing where you're going. (Continue: the errand-less walk as one of the last unproductive acts; everything else in the day has a destination; the purposeless walk is small rebellion.)

Then: the body has a native speed — three miles an hour. Everything since has been an argument with that number. The horse, the sail, the wheel, the piston, the turbine. The argument mostly won; the mind never upgraded.

### II. It is solved by walking

Zeno's paradoxes; Diogenes stands and walks. The Latin tag. Some problems aren't solved by argument but by motion. Grief, anger, writer's block — the stalled problems. The tradition of pacing. Then Aristotle and the peripatetics.

### III. The engine of thought

Stanford study; mechanism speculations; the default mode network; walking as exactly the right amount of busy — the leash on the anxious watchdog of the body. Optic flow. The rhythm. Two beats per second-ish, close to resting heartbeat ratios? Careful — keep it as musing.

### IV. The great walkers

Darwin's sandwalk with flints. Dickens's night miles. Woolf's pencil. Wordsworth's 175,000 miles and composing in iambics. Kierkegaard's letter. Nietzsche. Thoreau's four hours and sauntering etymology.

### V. The connoisseur of streets

Flâneur; Baudelaire; Benjamin; the turtle; slowness as resistance; loitering as art; the difference between walking to arrive and walking to be somewhere. The city at walking speed is a book; at driving speed a channel surfed.

### VI. The long walkers

Pilgrimage. Bashō. The Camino. Songlines (hedged). Chatwin's nomad thesis. Muir's quote. The walk that is not measured in hours but weeks; what dissolves and what crystallizes on day ten. (I can speculate lyrically without personal claim.)

### VII. Who gets to wander

The flâneur's privilege. Women, night, the mental arithmetic. Walking while Black; loitering/vagrancy laws; same gait, different verdicts. Gandhi; marches as grammar; Selma. Walking as the politics of the unarmored body.

### VIII. The confiscated street

Jaywalking's origin; the street as former commons; suburbs without sidewalks; Cubitt's treadmill and Wilde; the gym as the place we pay to walk; mall walkers as the last flâneurs, heartbreaking and defiant.

### IX. The unscreened hour

Phones; the walk as last unmonetized attention; boredom as compost; grief walks — hospital corridors, the first walk after bad news; walking gives grief a direction. 

### X. Going in

Return to the door. The walk ends where it starts; you bring back nothing except rearranged furniture of the mind. Muir echo. End on the threshold crossed twice.

### I. The door

There is a particular pleasure in closing a door behind you without knowing where you're going. (Continue: the errand-less walk as one of the last unproductive acts; everything else in the day has a destination; the purposeless walk is small rebellion.)

### II. It is solved by walking

Zeno's paradoxes; Diogenes stands and walks. The Latin tag. Some problems aren't solved by argument but by motion. Grief, anger, writer's block — the stalled problems. The tradition of pacing. Then Aristotle and the peripatetics.

Stanford study; mechanism speculations; the default mode network; walking as exactly the right amount of busy — the leash on the anxious watchdog of the body. Optic flow. The rhythm. Two beats per second-ish, close to resting heartbeat ratios? Careful — keep it as musing.

Darwin's sandwalk with flints. Dickens's night miles. Woolf's pencil. Wordsworth's 175,000 miles and composing in iambics. Kierkegaard's letter. Nietzsche. Thoreau's four hours and sauntering etymology.

### V. The connoisseur of streets

Flâneur; Baudelaire; Benjamin; the turtle; slowness as resistance; loitering as art; the difference between walking to arrive and walking to be somewhere. The city at walking speed is a book; at driving speed a channel surfed.

### VI. The long walkers

Pilgrimage. Bashō. The Camino. Songlines (hedged). Chatwin's nomad thesis. Muir's quote. The walk that is not measured in hours but weeks; what dissolves and what crystallizes on day ten. (I can speculate lyrically without personal claim.)

The flâneur's privilege. Women, night, the mental arithmetic. Walking while Black; loitering/vagrancy laws; same gait, different verdicts. Gandhi; marches as grammar; Selma. Walking as the politics of the unarmored body.

Jaywalking's origin; the street as former commons; suburbs without sidewalks; Cubitt's treadmill and Wilde; the gym as the place we pay to walk; mall walkers as the last flâneurs, heartbreaking and defiant.

### IX. The unscreened hour

Phones; the walk as last unmonetized attention; boredom as compost; grief walks — hospital corridors, the first walk after bad news; walking gives grief a direction. 

### X. Going in

Return to the door. The walk ends where it starts; you bring back nothing except rearranged furniture of the mind. Muir echo. End on the threshold crossed twice.
